title: Host Saturation Prefetch Credit Model
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes a credit-based prefetch and admission-control model that coordinates KV-cache offload activity with host memory/PCIe saturation signals. The goal is to reduce host thrash and tail latency during periods of high egress/ingestion while preserving cache hit-rate and throughput. This is an operational-level design (implementation sketch + experiments) intended to complement the existing KV residency heuristics and host-swap playbooks.

Motivation / Problem statement:

We observe two problematic regimes in capacity-constrained hosts:
- Bursty sequence workloads where many large KV pages are demanded simultaneously (e.g., cold long-context requests / long multi-turn chat replay) leading to PCIe saturation and IO queue latency spikes.
- Steady-state pressure where the host allocator keeps prefetching until host memory reclaim becomes aggressive, causing repeated host<->GPU page churn (micro-swap loops).

Current heuristics (prefetch-on-miss + static host-prefetch-window + grace thresholds) reduce some cases but are brittle: they do not consider host-side IO queue depth, observed PCIe latency trend, or the current effective concurrency (in-flight RPCs and GPU worker counts). As a result we see higher tail latency and sometimes a severe drop in overall throughput during cluster-wide hotspots.

Goals:
- Primary: keep 95/99th token latency bounded during host-prefetch events (< target SLO) while maintaining as high a KV-cache hit rate as practical.
- Secondary: avoid oscillatory host swap behavior and reduce PCIe queue saturation events.
- Operational: model must be implementable in the runtime layer with bounded state and minimal cross-host coordination.

Non-goals:
- This design does not replace offline model quantization recommendations or host hardware changes. Not a solution for permanent overcommit.

Key concepts / glossary (brief):
- Prefetch credit: a lightweight token that authorizes a worker to initiate host-prefetch I/O (page load). Credits track budget available to avoid saturating host resources.
- Host saturation signal: a local metric derived from PCIe/NUMA latency, host reclaim events, and host memory pressure counters that indicates risk of I/O saturation.
- Admission window: per-worker sliding window that limits number of outstanding prefetches per request.
- Debt & backoff: mechanism where workers that consume credits incur a recovery period before they can request more credits to avoid repeated bursty prefetching.

Design overview:

1) Credit pool and local bookkeeping
- Each node maintains a small, node-local credit pool (C_total). C_total is proportional to the number of GPU workers and the node's observed PCIe bandwidth/latency profile. Default baseline: C_total = max(8, floor(0.5 * gpu_worker_count)).
- Credits are consumed when a worker decides to prefetch one or more KV pages from host. A prefetch action with N pages consumes ceil(N / P) credits (P = pages per credit, default 4).
- Credits auto-refill at a steady rate (r credits / sec) up to C_total. Refill rate adapts downwards when host saturation signals are active and can be ramped up during idle windows.

2) Host saturation signal & adaptive credit modulation
- The node synthesizes a saturation score in [0,1] from: PCIe completion latency moving-percentile (p95), host reclaim event rate, host free memory slope, and current IO queue depth. Weighting: p95 latency (0.45), io-queue depth (0.25), reclaim events (0.2), memory slope (0.1).
- If saturation_score > 0.6, reduce refill rate r := r * (1 - (saturation_score - 0.6)). If saturation_score > 0.85, additionally clamp immediate credit grants (emergency hold).
- Saturation_score is computed every sampling_interval (default 250ms) and smoothed with exponential decay (alpha=0.2) to avoid flip-flopping on short spikes.

3) Admission & prefetch policy per request
- On KV miss, worker does: check local admission window (owindow) and credit_avail. If credits >= cost and owindow permits, worker issues prefetch and decrements credits. Otherwise, fallback to blocking load-on-demand (synchronous fetch) or limited prefetch (single page) depending on criticality hints (see below).
- Criticality hints: fast-path requests (short-context/high-priority) attach a high-criticality flag that allows borrowing a small debt up to D_max credits. Borrowing increases debt_counter for that worker which reduces refill priority and must be repaid by no-prefetch intervals.

4) Debt accounting and repayment
- Borrowed credits create a debt TTL. Worker cannot borrow again until debt repaid to zero. Repayment occurs by scheduled pauses in credit consumption (e.g., next N seconds where prefetches are suppressed) or by gradually earning credits at a reduced rate. This prevents frequent small bursts from repeatedly hammering host IO.

5) PCIe vs UMA awareness and NUMA-specific thresholds
- For UMA (single-socket systems where host memory bandwidth/latency is uniform), the scoring weights favor PCIe p95; for NUMA machines we add a locality penalty when cross-node page fetches are detected and reduce C_total accordingly.
- Node categorization: during startup, node runs a micro-benchmark: small reads from device memory to measure p50/p95 PCIe latency and local-to-remote host memory copy latency. These bench profiles tag node with class {low-latency, medium, saturated-prone}. Default C_total and refill parameters are chosen from the profile.

6) Eviction coordination and graceful degradation
- When saturation_score is high and credits drop below a low-watermark (LWM, default 2), workers stop prefetching and instead: 
  * Serve from a smaller in-GPU working set (priority eviction compaction),
  * If a miss occurs, do an on-demand synchronous fetch and return partial/generated tokens if allowed (best-effort degraded mode).
- To avoid immediate mass-evictions, we introduce a staged eviction where only non-hot slabs are reclaimed first and hot slabs get a soft-touch heuristic (reduce prefetch probability instead of immediate eviction).

7) Mesh & cross-host coordination (optional / future)
- The above is intentionally local. A lightweight cross-host gossip (every 5s) of saturation summaries can be used by the scheduler to avoid routing more requests to nodes currently in high saturation. This is a low-bandwidth announcement: node-id, saturation_score, credit_slack. Implementation as an optional optimization.

Metrics to drive tuning & experiments:
- Prefetch credit utilization (%) and refill-reduction events per minute.
- PCIe p95 before/after credit changes.
- Host reclaim count and host swap churn (pages/sec moved).
- Request tail latencies (95/99th token latencies) during prefetch windows.
- KV hit-rate delta during credit clamps (measure degradation).

Experiment plan (initial):
1) Canary on staging fleet: roll credit-based model but keep traditional prefetch as fallback; route 10% of production-like traffic for 48 hours. Observe saturation triggers and tail latency.
2) A/B on synthetic bursty workloads: generate concurrent long-context requests and compare: baseline, credit model with conservative C_total, aggressive C_total. Collect p95/p99 and throughput.
3) NUMA vs UMA bucketed test: verify that the node-classification picks reasonable defaults and that cross-node fetch penalty reduces prefetch volume.

Implementation notes / runtime concerns:
- Keep all state node-local, compact: integer credits, float saturation_score, per-worker debt int, per-worker owindow counters. Persist metrics to existing tracing layer (span tags) for debugging.
- Sampling of PCIe p95: use hardware counters where available. Fallback to measuring kernel-level completion latency for host DMA reads.
- Page-size accounting: standardized to host-page units (e.g., 2MB slab/page) to avoid mismatches across platforms.

Rollout / operational playbook:
- Start in "observe" mode where credits are simulated (no enforcement), record recommended actions for two weeks and tune parameters.
- Move to "enforce" in canary capacity; keep config flags to disable credit enforcement per-node.
- Monitoring alerts: saturationscore > 0.9 for > 30s; credit utilization > 95% with sustained high PCIe p95; mass reclaim events > threshold.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Exact mapping of pages-per-credit (P) and refill rate (r) needs hardware-specific calibration. Too coarse credits reduce flexibility; too fine increases bookkeeping overhead.
- Interaction with global schedulers and routing: should the global router avoid saturated nodes proactively? This doc keeps node-local scope to simplify initial rollout.
- Debt semantics: should debt be transferable between workers on the same node? Right now it's per-worker to simplify fairness.

Short TODOs:
- [ ] Add micro-benchmark runner to node bootstrap to classify node class. (JIRA:SRV-1451)
- [ ] Implement credits counters + refill loop in worker process. (PR sketch: /pull/760)
- [ ] Add PCIe/host metrics exporters and new tracing tags.
- [ ] Prepare staging canary and synthetic workload generator.

Appendix: simple pseudo flow for a worker on KV miss:

1) on_kv_miss(key, pages_needed):
   if local_credits >= ceil(pages_needed / P) and owindow < OW_MAX:
      consume credits; send async prefetch; increment owindow; attach request_id to prefetch;
   else if can_borrow and criticality==high:
      borrow credits up to D_max; schedule debt TTL; send prefetch;
   else:
      do synchronous fetch (blocking) and mark sample for tracing;

2) on_prefetch_complete(request_id):
   decrement owindow; if hit then update working-set recency; if miss then mark failure metric;

Notes for reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative: start with small default credit pools and tune up. The modeling can be extended later to make credit pools proportional to observed sustained throughput (moving average).
- Looking for feedback especially on: debt semantics, sampling intervals for saturation, and whether the node-class micro-bench should run at boot or on demand.

Authors / reviewers:

End of doc.
